title: Spelling's Glow-Up: Rebuilding Instruction from the Ground Up
author: Samantha Lippert
summary: Samantha Lippert describes how she is rebuilding spelling instruction in her Wonders-based ELA block after two years of reworking fluency, vocabulary, and text-based work. Working within district constraints that require a separate spelling grade, nightly homework, and curriculum-provided lists, she keeps the spelling notebook and weekly test but adds daily word dictation on mini whiteboards, weekly sentence dictation, and partner checking. Drawing on Science of Reading podcasts with Brennan Chandler and Sean Morrisey, she redesigns homework so each night uses a different strategy: word mapping, word sums, word chaining, and cover-copy-compare. She reports early signs of engagement, including families debating whether ricey is a real word. Her stated goal is transfer into daily writing, which she plans to track with a spelling inventory at benchmark points.
points: Lippert's district constraints mean the weekly spelling test stays, but it is no longer the whole of spelling instruction.
Daily dictation of six to eight list words applies the same retrieval logic that works for fluency and math facts.
Sentence dictation once a week forces students to hold phonics patterns, syntax, and mechanics together in working memory.
Each homework night targets a different mechanism, from grapheme mapping to morphology through word sums.
A spelling inventory at benchmarks will classify errors as phonetic, morphological, or orthographic to target instruction.
quotes: Each week brought a spelling list built around a phonics skill — better than just a random list of words, sure, but the accompanying activities did little to actually build my students’ spelling skills.

Every day, all students practice 6–8 words from their weekly list on mini whiteboards. I’ve seen how powerful daily practice is for moving knowledge into long-term memory with both fluency and math facts — spelling deserves the same treatment.

One day a week, we’ll shift from single words to sentence dictation. This will help students hold phonics patterns, syntax, and writing mechanics in working memory simultaneously helping to move spelling out of isolation and into authentic writing contexts.
Quite a few parents hadn’t thought “ricey” was a real word and had turned to AI to check. Those conversations are exactly what I want to hear.
My goal is simple: transfer. I want to see this orthographic mapping show up in their daily writing, not just on our Friday quiz.

I’ll repeat this inventory at our benchmark points throughout the year to track growth over time and analyze error patterns (e.g., phonetic vs. morphological vs. orthographic rule errors) to target instruction where it’s needed most.
